rationale: Start with a broad gradient ending at high organic strength to locate the elution window while minimizing truncation risk. The retention and resolution pattern will guide subsequent focusing of the gradient and temperature adjustments.

Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test selectivity of the sole unresolved pair (R = 0.87). The current elution window leaves ample margin below 10 minutes, so improving this pair could reach the maximum CRF.

The central peak pattern suggests an elution-order reversal between 40 and 50 C; a further 5 C increase may open that critical separation. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate this effect while checking the neighboring pair, whose resolution decreased at 50 C.

Make the gradient shallower at 55 C to improve the remaining critical separation (R = 1.29) while preserving the newly resolved central pair. The current last peak at 7.25 minutes provides room to increase separation without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The maximum CRF has been reached; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. This intermediate slope should improve the marginal central pair relative to 16 minutes while retaining sufficient separation for the pair that failed at 12 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek earlier elution while slightly reducing gradient slope. Check whether both critical pairs remain above R = 1.5; injection 5 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction restores the critical separation at the shorter 12-minute gradient. This reverses the selectivity loss seen when phi0 increased and may give full resolution with earlier last-peak elution than injection 5.

With a maximum-score method secured, explore lower-temperature selectivity using a shorter gradient. Cooling may separate the central cluster in a different elution order and reveal a faster fully resolved window.

Explore a faster high-temperature window where the previously critical pair may separate after reversing elution order. The stronger start and steeper gradient deliberately move beyond the near-coelution region, while checking for new losses elsewhere.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the remaining close pair separates further in the high-temperature elution order. Monitor the early peaks and the neighboring R = 1.62 pair for losses as retention shortens.

Test a steeper gradient to enlarge the reversed critical separation at 60 C, while lowering phi0 to protect the early peaks and neighboring central separation. This explores a substantially faster alternative to the confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a shorter gradient at intermediate temperature, using a weak start to preserve early and central separations. This checks whether slope changes can resolve the central cluster in the 40 C elution order without the neighboring-pair losses seen at 60 C.

Test one temperature step below the original 40 C run to move the central critical pair away from its apparent crossover. Keeping the original gradient isolates temperature selectivity and checks whether neighboring separations remain adequate.

Refine around the fastest fully resolved method with a modest slope increase from 0.075 to 0.080 organic fraction per minute. This tests whether elution can be shortened further before the marginal separation falls below R = 1.5.

Test a shallower gradient at 40 C to open the central separation that limited injection 1. A stronger starting composition should offset some added retention, potentially yielding full resolution below 10 minutes in this alternative selectivity window.

Refine the promising 55 C region by making injection 6 one step shallower, aiming to raise its R = 1.10 pair above 1.5 while retaining the stronger central separation. This may provide another maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins and last-peak elution below 10 minutes.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 16 to lift its R = 1.41 separation above 1.5, with the other critical pair currently at 1.74. This targets a maximum-score method with better resolution margins while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving the 0.075-per-minute slope of injection 7, the fastest fully resolved run. The gradient should still cover the observed elution window, testing whether the unused high-organic portion can be removed without losing maximum CRF.

Test an intermediate slope between injections 3 and 5 by lowering the endpoint one grid step. This should bring the R = 1.29 pair near full resolution while potentially matching or improving the fastest maximum-score elution time.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.0667 to 0.065 per minute to lift injection 19's R = 1.47 pair above the threshold. This targets full resolution near 7.8 minutes, with a larger central-pair margin than the fastest confirmed method.

Refine between the fully resolved slopes of injections 5 and 20 to seek more balanced critical-pair margins while keeping elution near 8 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Shorten the fastest confirmed method by one gradient-time step to test the faster boundary directly. The critical separation is likely to deteriorate, but this checks whether a different central peak pattern can retain full resolution; injection 18 remains the fallback.

With the faster boundary established, refine injection 17 by slightly reducing its slope to improve the smaller critical-pair margin. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, potentially preserving maximum CRF with more balanced resolution.

Shorten injection 21's programmed gradient while preserving its fully resolving slope of 0.0625 per minute. The gradient ends at the outlet at 8.65 minutes, after the previously observed last peak at 8.00 minutes, so maximum CRF should be retained with a lower organic endpoint.
